coverage.learning_objective: Apply basic data-quality checks (completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy) to decide whether a simple dataset is fit for a stated purpose.

required_facts.statement: Data quality means whether a dataset is fit for the purpose it will be used for.
source_refs: uk_gov_data_quality_framework#Why do we need a data quality framework?

required_facts.statement: Completeness checks whether the records and values that should be present in the dataset actually are, rather than missing.
Uniqueness checks whether a record that should appear once (one entity, one row) is duplicated in the dataset.
Validity checks whether a column's values are in the range and format expected for that column.
Accuracy checks whether the data correctly matches the real-world thing it describes.

misconceptions.statement: Good-quality data does not have to be perfect.

teaching_blocks.content: Before trusting any conclusion drawn from the delivery-orders table, you need to ask whether the data itself is any good. Data quality means whether a dataset is fit for the purpose it will be used for -- not whether it looks tidy, but whether it can actually support the question you're asking of it.

Two checks look at what's missing or repeated. Completeness checks whether the records and values that should be present in the dataset actually are, rather than missing -- for example, an order row with no delivery time recorded at all. Uniqueness checks whether a record that should appear only once -- one entity, one row -- is duplicated in the dataset -- for example, the same order number showing up as two separate rows.

Two more checks look at whether the values themselves are trustworthy. Validity checks whether a column's values are in the range and format expected for that column -- a delivery time recorded as '-5 minutes' fails validity, because negative time isn't a valid delivery time. Accuracy checks whether the data correctly matches the real-world thing it describes -- an order logged as delivered to Lagos when the driver actually delivered it to Abuja is complete, unique and validly formatted, but still inaccurate.

Good-quality data does not have to be perfect. The goal of these checks isn't a flawless dataset; it's a dataset good enough to answer the question you actually have, using completeness, uniqueness, validity and accuracy as the specific things to look for.
Running through these checks on the delivery-orders table before analyzing it is what tells you whether you can trust what the numbers say next.

video_need.reason: Each check (completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy) is about spotting a specific kind of problem inside a real table. Watching someone scan an actual table and point at a blank cell, a duplicate row, an out-of-range value and a real-world mismatch makes the four checks concrete in a way that describing each one in prose alone doesn't fully convey.

segments.label: Data-quality dimensions explained one at a time: accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, uniqueness
segments.summary: Presents data quality dimensions as separate factors, each measuring one aspect of how suitable a dataset is for its intended purpose, and walks through them one by one. Accuracy means the data reflects real-life facts and is checked against trusted sources; completeness means the important details are all there; consistency means the same value agrees wherever it appears (a phone number with an international code in one system but not another); validity means values fit the required format or rules (a zip code with the right number of digits, a date in the right format); uniqueness means no duplicates, so one person is not billed twice. Stops before the next dimension, integrity.

segments.label: Data quality as fitness for purpose, shown on one phone-and-email marketing list
segments.summary: Describes data quality as keeping data useful for its intended business purpose, then runs one example, a spreadsheet of phone numbers and email addresses for a marketing campaign, through the checks. Accuracy: the contact details were recorded correctly. Completeness: no customer is missing a phone number or email. Validity: emails contain an @ symbol and phone numbers start with a country code. Uniqueness: no contact is repeated. Timeliness: year-old contact data would be useless. It also uses consistency to mean data moving between systems without being altered, for instance software adding a stray quotation mark to each email.

bridge_note.before: Watch how each check is tied to one concrete problem: a missing detail, a repeated entry, a badly formatted value. Caution: clip 1 says validity means 'accurate', and clip 2 uses 'consistency' for data passing between systems unchanged.
bridge_note.after: Keep the four checks separate: a value can pass validity yet fail accuracy (a well-formed phone number that belongs to someone else). The clips present fitness for purpose but never say data doesn't have to be perfect; it only has to be good enough for the question you're asking.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a small delivery-orders table with planted problems, flag each problem and name the check it fails.
practice_anchor.success: The learner flags the row with no delivery time as a completeness failure, the repeated order number as a uniqueness failure, the negative delivery time as a validity failure, and states what real-world information would be needed to confirm accuracy.

visual_anchor.purpose: A delivery-orders table with a blank cell, a repeated row and an out-of-range value visibly marked, each tagged with the check it fails.

teaching_notes: The four required checks (completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy) are the core; consistency and timeliness are optional enrichment facts and can be skipped or touched only briefly.
Keep each check's example tight -- one line each, same delivery-orders table throughout.

context.concept_name: Ask, inspect, clean, analyze, visualize, communicate

coverage.learning_objective: Describe the repeatable analysis workflow (clarify the question, inspect and clean the data, analyze it, visualize findings, then communicate them) and use it to structure a small analysis task.

required_facts.statement: A repeatable analysis process typically begins by clarifying the question or purpose, so both the analyst and whoever needs the answer share an understanding of what is being analyzed and why.
Before analysis, the data should be inspected and checked for quality, so quality problems are addressed as early as possible.
source_refs: uk_gov_data_quality_framework#3.1 Assess data quality at all stages of the lifecycle

required_facts.statement: Cleaning the data helps reduce quality problems such as duplication and inconsistent values.
Analyzing means examining the prepared data to answer the question; exploratory data analysis, for example, looks at the data to uncover its underlying structure and spot anomalies (unusual values).
Visualizing means turning data into plots or other graphics; exploratory data analysis relies mostly on such graphical techniques to gain insight into a dataset and reveal its structure.
The final stage of an analysis is communicating the findings, and how far they can be trusted, to the people who will use them, not merely producing the analysis itself.
This process is commonly iterative rather than strictly linear: earlier stages, such as inspecting or cleaning, may be revisited as later stages reveal new issues.

teaching_blocks.content: Once you know how to read the delivery-orders table and check its quality, the next question is what order to actually do things in. A repeatable analysis process typically begins by clarifying the question or purpose -- for the delivery data, that might be 'which cities have unusually slow deliveries?' Clarifying this first means both you and whoever asked for the analysis share an understanding of what is being analyzed and why, before any work starts.

Next comes inspecting and cleaning. Before analysis, the data should be inspected and checked for quality, so problems are addressed as early as possible -- this is where quality checks such as completeness, uniqueness, validity and accuracy from before come in. Cleaning the data then helps reduce quality problems such as duplication and inconsistent values, for example removing the duplicate order row you found during inspection.

With the data prepared, you analyze it: examining the prepared data to answer the question. Exploratory data analysis, for example, looks at the data to uncover its underlying structure and spot anomalies -- unusual values, like one delivery that took far longer than every other delivery in the batch. For the delivery data, analyzing might mean looking closely at the cleaned rows to see which cities' deliveries stand out.

Visualizing is its own step: turning data into plots or other graphics. Exploratory data analysis relies mostly on such graphical techniques to gain insight into a dataset and reveal its structure, but making the graphic is a different job from examining the data. For the delivery data, visualizing might mean turning those delivery times into a graphic so the pattern is easy to see at a glance.

The final stage is communicating the findings, and how far they can be trusted, to the people who will use them -- not merely producing the analysis itself. Telling a manager 'Lagos deliveries are running slow, but the sample is small' is part of the workflow, not an afterthought.

This process is commonly iterative rather than strictly linear: earlier stages, such as inspecting or cleaning, may be revisited as later stages reveal new issues -- if analyzing the delivery data turns up a value that looks wrong, you go back and inspect or clean it before continuing, rather than treating each stage as done for good.

video_need.reason: This is a multi-stage workflow with a loop back into earlier stages -- exactly the kind of process relationship that a diagram of the stages, with the iterative loop drawn in, makes easier to hold in mind than prose describing the same stages in sequence.

media.group_title: One analysis from question to findings

segments.label: One analysis walked through in order: ask, prepare, clean, analyze, share
segments.summary: Follows one real analysis, an employee engagement survey, through its stages. First ask what problem is being solved and what the stakeholders hope to learn. Then prepare: decide what kind of data is needed and whether it must be collected or already exists. Then clean, treated as a first look at the data's structure plus quality-assurance questions about missing data, correct coding and unusual values. Then analyze, running the analyses planned from the original questions while letting the data speak rather than confirming a hunch. Finally share the findings, starting with high-level results for the executive team.

bridge_note.before: Watch how everything after the stakeholders' question (what data to collect, which checks to run, which analyses to run) follows from it. Her 'prepare' stage (deciding on and collecting data) is not a Devspace step; her 'clean' includes what Devspace calls inspecting.
bridge_note.after: The clip walks one straight line from question to sharing and does not show visualizing as a separate step or looping back to earlier stages. Devspace keeps analyze and visualize distinct and treats the process as iterative: a surprise in the analysis can send you back to inspect or clean. The clip also says to share findings but not how far they can be trusted, which Devspace includes in communicating.

practice_anchor.objective: Put the steps of a small delivery-data analysis in order (clarify the question, inspect, clean, analyze, visualize, communicate), then say where the process loops back when the analysis turns up a suspicious value.
practice_anchor.success: Steps are in the correct order with analyze and visualize kept distinct, and the learner points back to inspecting or cleaning as the step to revisit.

visual_anchor.purpose: The six workflow stages in order, with a visible loop from later stages back to inspecting and cleaning.

teaching_notes: Keep 'analyze' and 'visualize' as clearly distinct steps -- don't let visualize collapse into analyze; this path splits them explicitly.
The iterative note (going back to inspect/clean) should stay a short closing point, not a new sub-workflow.

context.concept_name: Data ethics, privacy, and responsible handling basics

coverage.learning_objective: Apply basic data-ethics and privacy principles (respecting privacy, minimizing collection, honest reporting of limitations) when handling and presenting data in a small analysis task.

required_facts.statement: Data users should respect the privacy and confidentiality of the individuals a dataset describes.
Responsible data handling includes minimizing data collection to what is needed and being accountable for how the data is used.
Data work should consider its potential impact on the people and communities it affects.
When sharing data and findings, data users should honestly report data limitations and known biases rather than overstating certainty.
Identifying information that isn't needed for the purpose should be left out or removed, especially before data is shared; findings can describe a group without identifying individuals.

misconceptions.statement: Removing identifying information does not by itself remove the risk of re-identification; the data combined with other available data can still identify people.

teaching_blocks.content: The delivery-orders table almost certainly contains information about real people -- customers' addresses, drivers' names. Data users should respect the privacy and confidentiality of the individuals a dataset describes, which means treating that table as more than just numbers to analyze.

Responsible data handling includes minimizing data collection to what is needed and being accountable for how the data is used -- if the analysis only needs delivery times and cities, there's no reason to collect or keep customers' phone numbers. Data work should also consider its potential impact on the people and communities it affects: a finding like 'deliveries to this neighborhood are consistently late' could affect real customers and drivers, not just look interesting in a report.

When sharing data and findings, data users should honestly report data limitations and known biases rather than overstating certainty -- if the delivery data only covers one week, or one driver logged times inconsistently, that limitation belongs in the report, not left out to make the conclusion sound stronger than it is. Identifying information that isn't needed for the purpose should be left out or removed, especially before data is shared; findings can describe a group without identifying individuals -- reporting 'the eastern delivery zone runs slow' rather than naming individual customers.

Removing identifying information does not by itself remove the risk of re-identification: the data, combined with other available data, can still identify people, so removing a name column alone isn't automatically enough.
Treating the people behind the delivery-orders data with care, and being honest about what the analysis can and can't claim, is as much a part of the job as getting the numbers right.

video_need.reason: These are principles and judgment calls -- privacy, minimization, honest reporting, the limits of de-identification -- stated and grounded in the delivery-orders example through text. There is no mechanism, tool or changing state to show, so a video would only restate the same points in another voice.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a delivery table and a stated purpose, choose which columns to keep and which to leave out before sharing, and note one limitation to report.
practice_anchor.success: Columns not needed for the purpose, such as customer phone numbers and names, are left out; the learner also notes that removing them does not fully rule out re-identification, and names one data limitation to state in the findings.

teaching_notes: Keep ethics principles grounded in the same delivery-orders example, not abstract.
The de-identification misconception (m1) is easy to skip -- make sure it's stated explicitly, not implied.

context.concept_name: Identifying the business decision a stakeholder needs the analysis to inform

coverage.learning_objective: Identify the business decision that a stakeholder's analysis request is meant to inform.

required_facts.statement: Analysis is the collection, manipulation and interpretation of information and data for use in decision-making.
The engagement and scoping stage of an analytical project should establish an understanding of how the analysis will inform decisions.

teaching_blocks.content: An operations manager emails you: "Can you look into our delivery times?" Before opening a notebook, the first thing worth asking is not what to measure, but what decision this is actually for.

Analysis is the collection, manipulation and interpretation of information and data for use in decision-making. A request for analysis often exists because someone needs to decide something, even when the request itself doesn't say so directly.

The engagement and scoping stage of an analytical project should establish an understanding of how the analysis will inform decisions. For the delivery-times request, that can mean asking the manager directly: is this about deciding whether to hire more couriers for the Lagos route, whether to renegotiate with a courier partner, or something else? The answer changes what you'd actually need to measure.

Naming the decision up front -- "this analysis is meant to help decide whether to add Lagos couriers" -- gives everything that follows a target to aim at, rather than leaving you to guess what "look into it" was supposed to produce.

video_need.reason: This is a reasoning habit conveyed through a worked request-to-decision example in prose; there is no diagram, code, or process to watch.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a vague stakeholder request, state the specific decision it is meant to inform.
practice_anchor.success: The learner produces a single sentence naming the underlying decision (e.g. 'This analysis is meant to help decide whether to renegotiate with the courier partner'), not a restatement of the request or a list of metrics.

teaching_notes: Opens the stakeholder-communication thread's running scenario: an operations manager's delivery-times request, carried through later concepts in this tile group.

context.concept_name: Stating a finding precisely and quantitatively (the specific number or comparison, not a vague claim)

coverage.learning_objective: State an analysis finding as a specific, complete claim that accurately reflects what the data shows, rather than a vague summary.

required_facts.statement: A communication's big idea must articulate a unique point of view, convey what's at stake, and be a complete sentence.

A claim about the data should be checked against what the data actually shows, and narrowed if needed; one article's example revises the broader claim 'Price has declined for all products' to the more precise 'the average retail price of existing products declined' once the underlying data was examined more closely.
Writing about data should be specific about the point being made.

Putting data into context includes making comparisons, for example: 'There were 787,000 suspensions in the 2022/23 academic year. This is an increase from the previous year, when 578,300 suspensions occurred...'

teaching_blocks.content: Once you've analyzed the delivery data, "delivery times went up" is a finding of sorts, but it doesn't say by how much, where, or compared to what.

A communication's big idea must articulate a unique point of view, convey what's at stake, and be a complete sentence -- not a fragment or a topic label. "Lagos delivery times" is only a topic label. "Lagos delivery times have risen, so customers on that route are waiting longer for their orders" is a complete sentence that takes a position (Lagos has slowed down) and says what's at stake (customers waiting longer).

A claim about the data should be checked against what the data actually shows, and narrowed if needed; one article's example revises the broader claim "Price has declined for all products" to the more precise "the average retail price of existing products declined" once the underlying data was examined more closely. The same check applies to the delivery claim: if only Lagos routes actually slowed down, "delivery times went up" should narrow to "Lagos delivery times went up", not describe every city.

Writing about data should be specific about the point being made, and putting data into context includes making comparisons -- for example: "There were 787,000 suspensions in the 2022/23 academic year. This is an increase from the previous year, when 578,300 suspensions occurred..." Following that same pattern, a precise delivery finding names the number and the comparison: "the average Lagos delivery time rose to 30 minutes this month, up from 22 minutes last month," rather than just "delivery times went up."

video_need.reason: Precision in a written claim is demonstrated by rewriting a vague sentence into a specific one -- a text-and-example skill with no visual component.

practice_anchor.objective: Rewrite the vague finding 'sales went up' as a precise, quantified statement that names a specific number and a comparison to a prior period.
practice_anchor.success: The rewritten statement is a complete sentence, names at least one specific number, and includes a comparison (e.g., to a previous month or year), with no vague qualitative language remaining.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a vague finding sentence alongside its rewritten precise version so the learner can see exactly what changes when a number and comparison are added.

teaching_notes: Optional enrichment (quality assurance of communications, f1) is skipped -- not required for this concept's coverage.

context.concept_name: Converting a vague business question into a specific, measurable analytical question

coverage.learning_objective: Convert a vague business question into a specific analytical question with agreed boundaries and precision, that can actually be answered with data.

required_facts.statement: In the engagement and scoping stage, the analyst should engage with the commissioner to identify the question, the context, and the boundaries of the analysis, as well as constraints such as deadlines and available resources.
The engagement and scoping stage should lead to agreement between the analyst and commissioner about the outputs of the work, including acceptable levels of accuracy, precision and margins of error.

A well-formed statistical question makes clear the variable(s) of interest, the group it focuses on, and its intent — describing the data, comparing a variable across two or more groups, or looking at an association between two variables — and can be answered with data collected or already in hand.

teaching_blocks.content: "Are deliveries going well?" is the kind of question a stakeholder might actually ask -- and it can't be answered with data as written.

In the engagement and scoping stage, the analyst should engage with the commissioner to identify the question, the context, and the boundaries of the analysis, as well as constraints such as deadlines and available resources. That kind of conversation can turn "are deliveries going well" into something answerable: which cities, which time period, compared against what.

A well-formed statistical question makes clear the variable(s) of interest, the group it focuses on, and its intent -- describing the data, comparing a variable across two or more groups, or looking at an association between two variables -- and can be answered with data collected or already in hand. "Is average delivery time in Lagos this month higher than last month?" names the variable (delivery time), the group (Lagos, this month vs. last), and the intent (a comparison) -- unlike the original vague question.

The engagement and scoping stage should lead to agreement between the analyst and commissioner about the outputs of the work, including acceptable levels of accuracy, precision and margins of error, so both sides know in advance what kind of answer will count as sufficient.

video_need.reason: Turning a vague question into a measurable one is demonstrated through a worked rewrite in text; there is nothing to watch that a comparison of the two question forms doesn't already show.

practice_anchor.objective: Turn the vague question 'are we doing well?' into a specific, measurable analytical question by identifying the variable of interest, the group it focuses on, and the intent of the question.
practice_anchor.success: The learner produces a rewritten question that names at least one measurable variable, specifies the group or time period, and states a clear intent (description, comparison, or association) — and can explain what scoping conversation would be needed to arrive at it.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a vague business question ('Are we doing well?') alongside a rewritten well-formed statistical question, with annotations labelling the variable of interest, the group, and the intent in the rewritten version.

coverage.learning_objective: Identify a stakeholder's requirements (scope, constraints, and expected output) before starting an analysis, and capture them in a specification.

required_facts.statement: In the engagement and scoping stage, the commissioner should inform the analyst about the important aspects of the problem, its scope, and any constraints or issues.

The analyst should create a specification document that captures the commissioner's requirements, providing a definition of the scope and project constraints; the analyst should share this specification with the commissioner for sign-off.
The commissioner should communicate to the analyst any relevant information about data sources and data quality.
Constraints around resources and timelines should be clarified and agreed between the analyst and commissioner during engagement and scoping.
The engagement and scoping stage should lead to agreement between the analyst and commissioner about the outputs of the work.

teaching_blocks.content: Agreeing on the decision and the question still leaves open what you actually need from the operations manager before you can start: what data, by when, in what form.

In the engagement and scoping stage, the commissioner should inform the analyst about the important aspects of the problem, its scope, and any constraints or issues, and should communicate to the analyst any relevant information about data sources and data quality -- for the delivery request, that could mean telling you which system holds delivery timestamps and whether any routes are missing GPS data.

Constraints around resources and timelines should be clarified and agreed between the analyst and commissioner during engagement and scoping -- for instance, whether the manager needs an answer this week or can wait for a fuller analysis next month.

The analyst should create a specification document that captures the commissioner's requirements, providing a definition of the scope and project constraints; the analyst should share this specification with the commissioner for sign-off -- for the delivery request, a short written specification of the routes, time period, data source, and deadline, which the manager signs off. The engagement and scoping stage should lead to agreement between the analyst and commissioner about the outputs of the work -- for instance, agreeing the deliverable is a one-page summary with a bar chart of average delivery time per city.

video_need.reason: Requirements-gathering is a checklist-style conversation habit explained adequately in prose, with no visual or procedural element to demonstrate.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a short stakeholder request, list the four requirement categories (data needed, scope, deadline, output format) and write one concrete question the analyst should ask the commissioner to clarify each category before starting.
practice_anchor.success: The learner produces a list that names all four categories, assigns a realistic clarifying question to each, and does not begin any analytical work until all four are addressed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the engagement-and-scoping stage as a two-way exchange: commissioner provides problem context, scope, constraints, and data-quality information → analyst drafts specification document → commissioner signs off → both parties agree on outputs before analysis begins.

clusters.title: Data Quality and the Analysis Workflow
clusters.reasoning: Data quality is a prerequisite concern that feeds directly into the analysis workflow — understanding what makes data trustworthy is part of understanding the workflow itself. These two concepts read as steps of one process. Ethics/privacy is a distinct conceptual domain (legal and ethical obligations) that learners must learn to separate from the technical workflow, so it is not clustered here.

clusters.title: Identifying Decisions, Findings, and Requirements
clusters.reasoning: Identifying the decision need, stating findings precisely, framing the analytical question, and identifying requirements are four sequential steps of the same pre-analysis phase: understanding what the stakeholder actually needs before any data is touched. They read as one process — scoping the work — and are always addressed together in stakeholder conversations. Each step builds on the previous one.
